# Chapter 1: From Tough Coaches, Tough Parents, and Tough Guys to Finding Real Inner Strength

## The Traditional View of Toughness

When college students described toughness, words like "hard-nosed," "gritty," "playing through pain," "stoic," and "persevering" came to mind. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. The traditional image: a football player popping a dislocated shoulder back into place, or Craig MacTavish, the last NHL player without a helmet (retired 1997). Most picture overcoming adversity and pain—a strong brute of a man.

## Bobby Knight's Model

Bobby Knight won over 900 games (third most all-time), reached five Final Fours, and won three NCAA championships. His 1976 Indiana team went undefeated, pioneering a pressing man-to-man defense. Knight defined toughness as "being able to overcome obstacles. You can't feel sorry for yourself." His methods included: hanging tampons from lockers of players he thought "soft," cussing out players, a 1991 tirade ("I'll fucking run your ass right into the ground"), bringing toilet paper with feces to show what he thought of them, and choking a player at practice. All in the name of creating toughness founded on showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear for authority and control—an idea still dominating playing fields.

## Authoritarian Parenting

Developmental psychologist Diana Baumrind (1960s) classified parenting by two factors: responsiveness (fostering individuality, self-regulation, and self-assertion through attunement and support) and demandingness (maturity demands, supervision, discipline, and willingness to confront disobedience). Three categories emerged: permissive (low demandingness, high responsiveness), authoritarian (high demandingness, low responsiveness), and authoritative (high demandingness, high responsiveness). Authoritarian parents don't trust children to make good decisions; they rely on fear, threats, and punishment. In one study of over 1,000 parents, only 31% of authoritarian parents said they should "love their child unconditionally." 81% of Americans thought parents were too soft. The "just right" fit occurs when expectations are high but so is support—high demand with warmth and understanding.

## The Callous Model

Toughness has been tied to masculinity and machismo—"man up," "stop being a pussy," "there's no crying in baseball." In youth sports, children run laps or do burpees not for training adaptation but to "toughen them up." In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found frequent vomiting after workouts and insult-laden tirades; parents justified teaching eleven-year-olds to go until they puke as "necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior."

## Consequences of the Old Model

On May 29, 2018, University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair (19) showed profound fatigue during ten 110-yard sprints—bending over, cramping. Coaches yelled to "get him the [expletive] up" and "drag his [expletive] across the field." It took 34 minutes to get him off the field, another 28 to call 911—1 hour 28 minutes total. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. Rhabdomyolysis, once rare, has become common from extreme workouts designed not to improve fitness but to "test" athletes—as Ohio University professor B. David Ridpath described, to "toughen up the current players or weed out a few to open some scholarship slots."

Authoritarian parenting leads to lower independence, more aggressive behavior, higher substance abuse and risky behaviors. In sport, it's linked to lower grit, increased emotional exhaustion, burnout, and fear of failure. In a study of over 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to higher child misbehavior. In the Israeli military, those from authoritarian environments coped worse than peers from nurturing environments. The authoritarian style creates the appearance of discipline without fostering it. One young athlete explained: "Coaches use exercise as punishment because they want you to become stronger... I need to work harder because I don't want to be punished." He didn't want to work harder to get better or win—he wanted to avoid punishment.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, based on appearance over substance. It's Bobby Knight losing control and throwing tantrums, the bully at school, the executive masking insecurity by yelling, the strength coach who works athletes so hard they get injured.

Real toughness: "experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It's navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can." Not bulldozing or pushing through, but navigating—sometimes going through, around, under, or waiting until it passes.

## Pete Carroll's Alternative

Pete Carroll, one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl, encourages meditation and yoga, shifts from meetings to ring toss if players get heated. According to one star player: "He's never negative, doesn't scream. He finds a way to turn a mistake into a positive." Carroll believes toughness comes from inner drive, embracing challenges, and bouncing back. He told *The Bleacher Report*: "Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they've been prepared to do." Other successful humanistic coaches: Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy (NFL); John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, Mike D'Antoni (basketball). As Ken Reed (*Ego vs. Soul in Sports*) summarized: "For every Lombardi or Bobby Knight you give me, I can give you an equally successful—if not more successful—humanistic coach." A 2008 study of nearly 200 basketball players concluded: "The 'keys' to promoting mental toughness do not lie in this autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive style. It appears to lie, paradoxically, with the coach's ability to produce an environment, which emphasizes trust and inclusion, humility, and service."

## The Author's Personal Experience

The author collapsed during a mile race due to paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)—vocal cords malfunctioning, shutting when they should open. The American Thoracic Society cites "strong emotions" and stress as triggers. His old strategy of pushing until he puked backfired. He had to learn to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady at the exact moment discomfort was highest.

## The Four Pillars

1. Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality
2. Listen to Your Body
3. Respond Instead of React
4. Transcend Discomfort

# Organizing: Setting Up the Right Buckets

## Basic Categories and Hard Edges
Seven primary types: Projects list, project support material, calendar actions/information, Next Actions lists, Waiting For list, reference material, Someday/Maybe list. Categories must be kept visually, physically, and psychologically separate. If reference materials mix with things to read, "you'll go unconscious to the stack." If calendar items blend with Next Actions, you won't trust your calendar.

All you need are lists and folders. A list can be: (1) file folder with separate paper notes, (2) titled paper in loose-leaf organizer, or (3) software inventory. Don't impose external priority scaffolding requiring rearranging — prioritize intuitively against shifting variables.

## Organizing Action Reminders

### Calendar Actions
Calendar shows only the "hard landscape" — time-specific ("10:00–11:00 meet with Jim") or day-specific ("Call Rachel Tuesday"). Resist putting actions on calendar that might need moving; keep calendar as sacred territory. Most actions belong in "as soon as possible" category.

### As-Soon-As-Possible Actions by Context
Organize by context (tool, location, situation). How discrete categories need to be depends on (1) number of actions and (2) how often contexts change. With 25 next actions, one list might suffice; with 50–100, you need sorting.

**Common list headings:**
- **Calls** — all phone calls; record phone numbers alongside each item. "Those strange little windows of time" (off-site, waiting) become usable.
- **At Computer** — actions needing computer. Author maintains separate **Online** list for actions requiring Wi-Fi (since he flies often). If mobile-centric, use single **Digital** context or fold into **Anywhere**.
- **Errands** — group reminders for out-and-about tasks. Sublists within items possible (e.g., "hardware store" with appended sublist). Location-based reminders are "overoptimistic" about technology; rigorous list still needed.
- **At Office** — actions requiring physical presence (e.g., purging filing cabinet). With "hotel-ing" (no permanent office), may need At Office A and B lists.
- **At Home** — actions only doable at home. "At Starbucks" can be a fine categorization.
- **Agendas** — items to cover with specific people or in standing meetings. Keep separate lists for bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorney, etc. Also for standing meetings (staff, board, parent/teacher). Add ad hoc as needed.
- **Read/Review** — longer-than-two-minute reading items. Best managed in a separate physical stack tray labeled "Read/Review." Some professionals need **Review/Respond** category. For digital input, create **Review/Watch** file or **Surf Web** action list.

### Organizing "Waiting For"
Track final deliverables or projects others are responsible for (e.g., tickets ordered, scanner coming, client approval). Include date requested and agreed-upon due date — "just this one tactical detail is worth its weight in gold." Keep list close to Next Actions; responsibility may bounce back and forth. Review list to assess if you need to check status.

### Using Original Item as Action Reminder
Exceptions: Read/Review articles (magazine itself as trigger), paper bills in "Bills to Pay" folder, receipts in "Receipts to Process" envelope. Caveat: "Just having them 'organized' isn't sufficient to get them off your mind." For e-mail: create **@ACTION** folder (prefix with @ or hyphen to sort at top) for longer-than-two-minute actionable e-mails; **@WAITING FOR** folder for delegated items (save cc/bcc copy). Getting e-mail in-tray to empty means deleting, filing, doing <2-min responses, moving actionable e-mails to @ACTION. "It takes much less energy to maintain e-mail backlog at zero than at a thousand."

**Caution about dispersing reminders:** You must review all categories equally. Digital data offscreen can disappear as viable prompt — "this has caused many computer-savvy people to revert to a paper planner."

## Organizing Project Reminders
Projects list is a comprehensive index of open loops (every commitment requiring >1 action step). Not for plans or priority sorting — you can't do a project, only action steps. Real value: complete review (at least weekly) ensuring action steps defined for all projects.

**Value of complete Projects list:**
- Critical for control and focus — "I've got to get my driver's license renewed" can take as much mental space as "I need to formulate the agenda for next year's conference."
- Alleviates subtle tensions — small things morph into bigger ones (e.g., preschool registration problems, invoice disputes).
- Core of Weekly Review — linchpin for marrying larger commitments to day-to-day.
- Facilitates relationship management — enables negotiation of explicit/implicit agreements with bosses, staff, partners.

**Where to find hidden projects:**
1. Current activities — calendar meetings, action lists, workspaces (e.g., conference call about client request → "Look into possible custom program for Client XYZ").
2. Higher-horizon interests — professional goals, company objectives, strategic plans, personal life (kids/parents aging, retirement).
3. Current problems, issues, opportunities — problems (always projects), process improvements, creative/capacity-building opportunities. Examples: "Look into improving Frederick's relationship with his school," "Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance," "Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner."

**One list or subdivided?** Most find one list best as master inventory. Subsorts: Personal/Professional (personal needs weekday review), Delegated Projects (for senior managers), Specific Types (e.g., "Projects—Presentations" chronological list for speakers), by major areas of focus. "The right amount of complexity is whatever creates optimal simplicity."

**Subprojects:** If big project has independent subprojects, list the big one on Projects list and hold subpieces in support material. Example: author moving from California to Europe — initially one project "Move to Amsterdam," later unpacked into fifteen (from "Set up Dutch bank accounts" to "Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara").

### Project Support Materials
Resources to support actions, not reminders. Don't use support material for reminding — stacks/files that haven't been processed deliver "incessant subliminal chant: 'Do something about me!'" Instead: add project to Projects list, put action steps on appropriate lists, pull support materials only when doing the action. For Weekly Review, pull project file to check for missing next actions.

**Organizing ad hoc project thinking:** Attached notes in software, e-mail reference folders (consider "Johnson Partnership—Active" and "Johnson Partnership—Archive"), paper-based files, pages in loose-leaf notebooks. Key: consistently look for action steps in notes, review notes as needed, clear out stale notes. "The inherent danger in the digital world is how much data can be spread into how many different places so easily, without coordinating links."

## Organizing Nonactionable Data

### Reference Materials
Once you've distinguished actionable from nonactionable, reference has "no pull or incompletion associated with it — it's just your library." Systems: general-reference filing (paper, e-mail, digital), large-category filing (topics needing >50 folders get own section), contact managers (purely reference — don't use for action reminders), libraries/archives at personalized levels. "If material is purely for reference, the only issue is whether it's worth the time and space to keep it."

### Someday/Maybes
Track things to reassess in future — "some of the most interesting and creative things you'll ever get involved with." Create Someday/Maybe list; populate from creative imaginings (hobbies, skills, trips, toys) and reassess current projects (move optional projects with no chance of attention for months). Subcategorize if useful (home projects vs. bucket-list fantasies). **Danger of "Hold and Review" files:** people hold but don't review; after processing, often nothing left.

**Using calendar for future options:**
- Triggers for activating projects (e.g., "Annual sales conference" reminder, key dates for birthdays)
- Events you might want to participate in (seminars, conferences)
- Decision catalysts — "It's OK to decide not to decide — as long as you have a decide-not-to-decide system." Major decisions: hire/fire, merge/acquire, change job/career, strategy redirection.

**Tickler file:** 43 folders — 31 daily (1–31) and 12 monthly. Daily files in front starting with tomorrow's date; after emptying, refile at back of dailies (becomes next month's date). Monthly files emptied into in-tray when they reach front, then refiled at back of monthlies. "It represents a unique executive function: deciding not to decide until a certain point." Must check and update every day.

## Checklists: Creative and Constructive Reminders
Checklists are "recipes of potential ingredients" for projects, processes, events, areas of responsibility. Alfred North Whitehead: "Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them." Use checklists for anything requiring regular refreshed view or specific detail you can't easily recall. Reference: Atul Gawande's *The Checklist Manifesto*.

**Things you want to pay attention to** (fuzzy commitments like "Exercise more regularly," "Maintain good morale on my team"): first identify inherent projects and actions. For things that don't fit, build overview checklists reviewed regularly — e.g., career goals, family, health, financial resources, creative expression. Within job: team morale, processes, timelines, staff issues, communications, technology.

**The more novel the situation, the more control required.** For new responsibilities (e.g., suddenly filling CEO shoes, new position, novel organizational structure), checklists are critical until things become automatic.

**Checklists at all levels:** Be open to creating any checklist — from "Core Life Values" to "Things to Take Camping" to "Potential Holiday Gifts." Examples: Job Areas of Responsibility, Exercise Regimens, Travel Checklist, Weekly Review, Training Program Components, Key Clients, People to Stay in Touch With, Year-end Activities, Personal Development, Jokes. "Capability and willingness to instantly make a checklist, accessible and used when needed, is a core component of high-performance self-management."
